statement: In US adults prescribed opioid painkillers — veterans in Veterans Health Administration care in 2004–2009 (mostly men; 2,400 overdose deaths in a case-cohort of 422,786 people) and privately insured people aged 18–64 in 2001–2013 (315,428 people) — time with a filled benzodiazepine prescription, compared with time on opioid prescriptions alone, is associated with more overdoses. Among the veterans, overdose deaths (any drug, any intent) occurred at 316 per 100,000 person-years during benzodiazepine prescription against 71 with none (unadjusted); the adjusted hazard ratio was 3.86 (95% CI 3.49–4.26), and 2.33 (2.05–2.64) for periods after a benzodiazepine prescription had ended. During benzodiazepine prescription the adjusted hazard rose with the prescribed daily dose, to 3.06 (2.38–3.92) for the highest against the lowest of five dose groups. Among the insured adults, the adjusted yearly share with an emergency visit or hospital admission for opioid overdose was 2.42% with at least one day of overlapping benzodiazepine and opioid prescriptions and 1.16% without (odds ratio 2.14, 2.05–2.24; 1.42 with occasional and 1.81 with long-term opioid prescriptions); that analysis did not adjust for opioid dose and counted only overdoses treated in hospital that people survived. Both studies measured pharmacy fills, not use; neither could see illicit drugs or medicines from other sources, or separate the medicine from the reasons it was prescribed (such as anxiety, depression or substance use), and the raised risk after prescriptions ended points to such differences or to continued use. Whether the combined risk exceeds what each drug carries alone was not tested, because everyone studied was receiving opioids; among the veterans the benzodiazepine association did not differ detectably by opioid dose (interaction P = 0.60). Whether benzodiazepines cause the excess is not shown.
plain: Are opioids plus benzos (such as diazepam or alprazolam) more dangerous? In two large US studies of people prescribed opioid painkillers, people who also had a benzo prescription had more overdoses. Among US veterans, about 3 in 1,000 died of an overdose each year while a benzo was prescribed, against fewer than 1 in 1,000 without one, and the risk was higher with higher prescribed benzo doses. Among insured adults aged 18 to 64, about 2 in 100 a year with both prescriptions went to hospital with an opioid overdose, against about 1 in 100 with opioids alone. The studies counted prescriptions, not what people actually took, and could not see street drugs. People given benzos often had more anxiety, depression or substance use problems, and the risk was also higher after their benzo prescription had ended, so part of the link may come from these differences rather than the medicine itself.
population: US adults with filled opioid painkiller prescriptions: veterans in Veterans Health Administration care, financial years 2004–2009 (case-cohort of all 2,400 overdose deaths and a 420,386-person random subcohort; 93% men, editors' calculation; methadone maintenance, buprenorphine and palliative or hospice care excluded) and privately insured adults aged 18–64 continuously enrolled in 2001–2013 (315,428; MarketScan claims; cancer excluded)
exposure: A filled benzodiazepine prescription during opioid prescription: current receipt by days' supply (veterans) or at least one day of overlap between benzodiazepine and opioid prescriptions in a calendar year (insured adults)
comparator: Time on opioid prescriptions without a benzodiazepine prescription: person-time never or not yet prescribed one (veterans); person-years without overlap (insured adults)
outcome: Death from overdose of any drug and any intent (National Death Index; veterans); emergency-room visit or hospital admission coded as opioid overdose in people who survived (insured adults)
magnitude: Veterans (Park et al., 2015): unadjusted overdose death rates per 100,000 person-years, scaled to the source population: no benzodiazepine 71 (95% CI 66–76), former receipt 187 (170–205), current receipt 316 (298–334); editors' calculation: a difference of 245 per 100,000 person-years, about 3.2 against 0.7 deaths per 1,000 person-years. Adjusted hazard ratios against none: current 3.86 (3.49–4.26), former 2.33 (2.05–2.64). Within current receipt, by daily dose as prescribed (diazepam equivalents; study conditions), against >0–10 mg: >10–20 mg 1.69 (1.42–2.01), >20–30 mg 2.34 (1.91–2.86), >30–40 mg 2.65 (2.10–3.33), >40 mg 3.06 (2.38–3.92). Hazard ratios for the highest against the lowest opioid dose group were similar without (3.30), after (3.00) and during (3.92) benzodiazepine prescription; interaction P = 0.60. Privately insured adults (Sun et al., 2017): adjusted annual share with a hospital-treated opioid overdose 2.42% (2.32–2.51) with against 1.16% (1.13–1.18) without overlap, odds ratio 2.14 (2.05–2.24); intermittent opioid prescriptions 1.45% against 1.02%, OR 1.42 (1.33–1.51); chronic (more than 10 prescriptions or more than 120 days' supply a year) 5.36% against 3.13%, OR 1.81 (1.67–1.96); in a broader sample enrolled for at least 2 years, adjusted relative risks 1.66 (1.64–1.69) and 1.61 (1.58–1.63).

evidence.locator: Results › Unadjusted rates of death from drug overdose, 1st paragraph; Table 2, benzodiazepine prescription history and daily dose rows
evidence.extracted: Of 2,400 overdose deaths, 1,185 (49%) occurred during current benzodiazepine prescription. Unadjusted overdose death rates per 100,000 person-years (estimates for the source population): none 71 (95% CI 66–76; 794 deaths), former 187 (170–205; 421 deaths), current 316 (298–334; 1,185 deaths); by prescribed daily benzodiazepine dose, >0–10 mg 152, >10–20 mg 301, >20–30 mg 518, >30–40 mg 600, >40 mg 805 (689–930). Editors' calculation: current against none, a difference of 245 per 100,000 person-years. The 0 mg/day row of Table 2 is internally inconsistent and is not used.

evidence.locator: Results › Adjusted analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 3, Models 1 and 2
evidence.extracted: Adjusted for sex, age, race, ethnicity, area poverty, time-varying opioid dose, recent substance-use admissions, Charlson index, diagnoses of substance use disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, other anxiety disorder, depression, bipolar or psychotic disorder and cancer, and other drug use: hazard ratio for overdose death 3.86 (3.49–4.26) for current and 2.33 (2.05–2.64) for former benzodiazepine receipt against none. Within current receipt, against >0–10 mg/day: 1.69 (1.42–2.01), 2.34 (1.91–2.86), 2.65 (2.10–3.33) and 3.06 (2.38–3.92) for >10–20, >20–30, >30–40 and >40 mg/day; temazepam against clonazepam 0.63 (0.48–0.82); dosing schedule not associated.

The interaction between benzodiazepine history and opioid dose was not significant (P = 0.60), which the authors describe as relations neither greater nor less than additive; in a Cox model this tests departure from multiplicative hazards (study card, reporting issue 1). Hazard ratios for ≥100 against >0–<20 mg morphine-equivalent per day: no benzodiazepine 3.30 (2.62–4.16), former 3.00 (2.19–4.11), current 3.92 (3.17–4.85).

evidence.locator: Methods › Study design and population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Deaths from drug overdose, 1st paragraph; Drug prescribing patterns, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Results › Sample, 1st paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: Case-cohort within VHA patients receiving outpatient opioid analgesics in financial years 2004–2009: 2,400 overdose deaths and 420,386 random controls (5% annual samples), 422,786 analysed after excluding methadone maintenance (221) and palliative or hospice care (5,816). Outcome: any intentional, unintentional or undetermined poisoning death by any drug (National Death Index). Exposure: person-days classified as current, former or no benzodiazepine receipt from fills and days' supply, doses computed as prescribed. 112,069 (27%) filled a benzodiazepine; they had more anxiety disorders (20% against 5%), post-traumatic stress disorder (22% against 9%), depression (38% against 19%) and substance use disorders (13% against 10%).

evidence.locator: Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses of study, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Findings in context, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors note veterans, mostly men; non-VHA prescriptions unseen; doses assume drugs were taken as prescribed; indications unknown. They say benzodiazepines go more often to people with substance misuse and psychiatric disorders, that residual confounding by their severity may remain, that the raised risk after prescriptions ended may reflect these conditions or continued illicit, outside or leftover benzodiazepines, and that half the deaths occurred without a benzodiazepine prescription.
evidence.quote: might be better conceptualized as a marker of risk

evidence.extracted: Adjusted annual incidence of an emergency-room visit or inpatient admission for opioid overdose: 1.16% (95% CI 1.13–1.18) without and 2.42% (2.32–2.51) with concurrent benzodiazepine use, odds ratio 2.14 (2.05–2.24); intermittent opioid prescriptions 1.02% against 1.45%, OR 1.42 (1.33–1.51); chronic opioid prescriptions 3.13% against 5.36%, OR 1.81 (1.67–1.96); adjusted for year, sex, age, the Table 1 comorbidities and prior health spending, with standard errors clustered by person.

evidence.locator: Methods › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Variables, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Analyses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: MarketScan claims, 2001–2013: 315,428 privately insured people aged 18–64, continuously enrolled for 13 years, without cancer, who filled an opioid prescription. Concurrent use: at least one day of overlap between opioid and benzodiazepine prescription intervals in a calendar year. Outcome: emergency-room visit or admission with codes for opioid poisoning or a potential opioid adverse event plus an opioid overdose code, during an opioid prescription interval or within 7 days. Covariates: age, sex, year, comorbidities and prior spending; opioid dose is not among them. Chronic opioid prescription: more than 10 prescriptions or more than 120 days' supply in a year.

evidence.locator: Results, 7th and 8th paragraphs; Discussion › Strengths and limitations of this study, 1st, 3rd and 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: In a broader sample of 3,810,747 people enrolled for at least 2 years, adjusted relative risks were 1.66 (1.64–1.69) for intermittent and 1.61 (1.58–1.63) for chronic opioid prescriptions. A residual-confounding analysis assumed a binary confounder in 75% of exposed and 0% of unexposed person-years. The authors state that unobserved confounding cannot be excluded, that only hospital-treated events in people who survived were counted, and that heroin and illegally bought prescription drugs are not captured.

risk_of_bias.note: Both studies ROBINS-E high on their cards: confounding by indication is not controlled (in the veteran study the hazard ratio after benzodiazepine prescriptions ended, 2.33, shows it may be large); the insured-adult analysis omits opioid dose and does not order the overlap and the overdose in time; both use fills, not use.

inconsistency.note: Same direction in both; the different sizes (hazard ratio 3.86 for deaths, odds ratio 2.14 for hospital-treated events) match different outcomes and adjustment sets.

indirectness.note: None as worded: each population, exposure definition and outcome is stated separately.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the veterans' adjusted hazard ratio (3.86) exceeds 2, but the remaining confounding (severity of the indication, unmeasured drug use) runs away from the null, as the raised hazard after prescriptions ended indicates (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Not applied: the veterans' adjusted gradient by prescribed benzodiazepine dose (1.69 to 3.06) is in the data, but in a between-person comparison higher prescribed doses plausibly track the same severity that confounds the main contrast, as the authors themselves say.

grade.reasoning: Two records-based cohorts in different US populations, read in full; observational, so they start low. Risk of bias −1 (both ROBINS-E high: uncontrolled confounding by indication, no opioid-dose adjustment in the insured-adult analysis, prescriptions as a proxy for use). Inconsistency 0, indirectness 0 as worded, imprecision 0; publication bias not assessable. Large effect and dose–response not applied (see the domain notes); a reading that credited the veterans' adjusted dose gradient would give low, and the strict reading gives very low. Relation: is associated with; the veteran study's authors themselves describe benzodiazepines as possibly a marker of risk, and causal wording would need designs that separate the medicine from the reasons it is prescribed. Status: replicated, by two independent teams in different populations with different outcomes (deaths; non-fatal hospital events). The claim does not say that the risks add or multiply: the veteran paper reads its interaction test as showing additivity, which misreads a Cox product term, and no study read compared benzodiazepines without opioids. A UK study of people in methadone or buprenorphine treatment is the subject of a separate answer.

verification.flag_note: The other Tier A cohorts for this cell (Dasgupta et al. 2016, Pain Med, 10.1111/pme.12907; Jones & McAninch 2015, Am J Prev Med, 10.1016/j.amepre.2015.03.040) have not been read; Hernandez et al. 2018 (exposure–response in Medicare, 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2018.0919) would test the dose–response question.
